item.title: When will life expectancy reach 100? No time soon
item.description:
Average expected lifespan is still increasing in high-income countries, but the rate of increase is slowing. People are living longer and longer lives than before, but the pace of growth in life expectancy has dropped sharply since the early twentieth century1.

item.title: Even dinosaurs weren’t safe from this giant croc-like predator
item.description:
The creature might have been more than 3.5 metres long, with powerful jaws and serrated, flesh-cutting teeth. A giant crocodile-like apex predator hunted large prey — probably including medium-sized dinosaurs — around 70 million years ago in what is now southern Argentina1.

item.title: Bright city lights make birds around the world sing longer
item.description:
Big-eyed species are especially vulnerable to the effects of light pollution, a citizen-science effort shows. Birds in brightly lit cities sing for an average of 50 minutes longer than those in the darkest environments, starting their vocalizations an average of 18 minutes earlier in the morning and finishing 32 minutes later in the evening, data from a global citizen-science effort show1.

item.description:
Cosmic maps appear consistent with the proposal that black holes could cause the Universe's accelerating expansion. An unorthodox explanation for dark energy fits with cosmological observations and better matches known properties of neutrinos than previous models do, calculations have shown1.

item.description:
Organ models with hallmarks of the disease show marked improvement when a protein’s levels are restored. A study of human brain organoids has revealed a new potential target for Alzheimer’s disease treatments1.

item.title: Water in the ‘Devil’s Comet’ shares a source with Earth’s oceans
item.description:
Chemical profiling traces the source of water in one of the brightest known comets to keep returning to the Solar System. Our home planet seems to share its heritage with a famous comet. By analysing the chemical make-up of the comet 12P/Pons-Brooks — which was discovered in 1812 and passes close to the Earth every 71 years — astronomers have deduced that its water comes from the same source as our own oceans1.

item.title: The world’s largest methane emitter manages to curb one source
item.description:
Output of the powerful greenhouse gas by China’s energy sector peaked in 2014, an inventory shows. China’s energy sector has cut its emissions of the potent greenhouse gas methane by 21% between 2014 and 2021, according to an inventory published this month1.

item.description:
Rat-sized carnivore called the ampurta makes speedy comeback despite unprecedented drought. A marsupial micro-predator native to Australia has overcome near-extinction in part thanks to its resilience during drought1.

item.title: Ancient coins unveil web of trade across southeast Asia
item.description:
Images on first-millennium coins hint at economic relationships across the region. Ancient silver coins that bear a rising sun and an ancient Indian religious symbol and that were found on opposite ends of southeast Asia suggest that there were extensive undocumented trade routes across the region1.

item.title: Super-efficient teamwork is possible — if you’re an ant
item.description:
The individual workers in a crew of 15 weaver ants exert more force than a single ant working alone. A special species of ant might hold the secret to effective teamwork. Researchers report that, as weaver ants (Oecophylla smaragdina) work in bigger and bigger groups to assemble nests, the efficiency of each team member also rises.

item.title: Mysterious coffee species turns out to be a blend
item.description:
A coffee variety called liberica, which is gaining popularity for the distinctive flavour of its beans, is actually three species. Detailed analysis of an obscure and resilient kind of coffee plant has revealed that it is, in fact, three separate species, each with attributes that could help to meet the world’s future caffeine demands1.

item.title: How animal paw pads got their toughness
item.description:
In creatures that walk on land, a protein called Slurp1 protects skin cells from stress. The skin on animals’ paws is versatile, providing traction on a variety of surfaces while also supporting a creature’s weight during running and jumping. Four-legged animals can thank a single protein that evolved to protect paw skin from mechanical pressure as creatures adapted to walking on land1.

item.description:
Ice coverage is shrinking on Heard Island — a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a haven of biodiversity. Over the course of more than seven decades, the yearly rate of glacier loss on Heard Island in the southern Indian Ocean has almost doubled, endangering largely pristine ecosystems at a United Nations World Heritage site1.

item.description:

item.title: Tiny motor uses heat to perform molecular magic
item.description:
A nanoscopic machine transforms a molecular chain into interlocking loops. The latest knitting craze is nanoscopic. Powered by light and heat, a tool called a molecular motor can twist strings of atoms into hard-to-break shapes called catenanes, chemists report1. The technique could be used to construct new kinds of molecule and material.

item.description:

item.title: Intricate origins of ice mummy’s ink revealed
item.description:
Imaging suggests that more than one tattooist applied pigment to the hands and forearms of a woman who lived more than two millennia ago. The Pazyryk people, who lived in the Altai Mountains of Siberia more than 2,000 years ago, are known for their intricate tattoos featuring animals in action. Now, a 3D scan of a mummy provides details of this body art, revealing for the first time some of the techniques used by these ancient tattooists1.

item.title: Lava planets’ atmospheres give away what lies beneath
item.description:
Modelling suggests that data collected by JWST will be able to distinguish between planets that are molten to the core and those that are not. Far-off ‘lava worlds’ might hide something beneath their magma surface. Astronomers say we might be able to tell how molten a distant planet is by studying its surface temperature and the chemicals in its atmosphere1.

item.description:
Warming in the Arctic shifts storm patterns, leading to reductions in wind speeds in places that rely on turbines for clean electricity. One-fifth of the world’s wind turbines are in areas where winds could drop for long periods in the future1.
